Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe

The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe is a distinct Ojibwe government in Minnesota. The Band’s historical overview, treaty explanation and illustrated Non-Removable Guide provide a community-authored introduction to its relationship with the Mille Lacs region. They connect migration accounts and seasonal food practices with treaties, removal pressure, land loss and the continuing assertion of self-government.

01

Community history and persistence

The Band’s public history traces its relationship to the Mille Lacs region and describes dispossession, boarding schools and the rebuilding of government. The inspected pages of the Non-Removable Guide place a community migration account and seasonal subsistence history alongside the Sandy Lake tragedy, removal pressure in the 1860s and later allotment. Read these publications as situated Band accounts rather than a single narrative for all Ojibwe governments. The guide is an illustrated introduction; only pages 2–5 were inspected, and the linked book-length Social History was not opened in the earlier review.

Read the sources [1] Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe [3] Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe

02

Treaties and the Band’s reading of retained rights

The Band’s treaty page distinguishes the 1837 land cession and retained hunting, fishing and gathering rights from the 1855 treaty establishing its reservation. It explains the Band’s account of federal litigation in the 1990s, the 1999 Supreme Court result and subsequent conservation-code practice. This makes a useful reading sequence from a treaty-era claim to later governmental action. Its legal summaries remain the Band’s interpretation and are not substituted for the actual treaty texts or reported opinions. The museum exterior accompanying this profile identifies a place devoted specifically to Mille Lacs Band history; no exhibit objects or design motifs are reproduced separately.

History — Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe ↗

Publication: Undated web page; page includes current institutional material

The Band’s own account traces its relationship to the Mille Lacs region, the 1837 and 1855 treaties, dispossession and later reconstruction of tribal government. This is a situated community history; broad legal summaries and undated population claims are not used as independently verified facts.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete History and Recognition of Self Government sections (page lines 87–113). The linked Social History of the Mille Lacs Band (1640–1993) was not opened or counted.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

Treaties — Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe ↗

Publication: Undated web page

This Band-authored reading explains its understanding of the 1837 ceded territory and retained hunting, fishing and gathering rights, and describes the 1994–1999 litigation and later conservation code. The Band’s legal interpretation is identified as its own account; the page is not a substitute for the treaty text or court opinions.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read the complete Treaty of 1837, Treaty of 1855 and Today sections (lines 51–76), including the Band’s account of the federal-court and Supreme Court proceedings.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026

The Non-Removable Guide — Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe ↗

Publication: Undated PDF; no publication date established from the inspected pages

The guide connects an Ojibwe migration account, seasonal food practices, treaties, the Sandy Lake tragedy, removal pressure, boarding schools and Band persistence. Claims and remembered history are presented as the Band’s account; this guide is related to the Band’s website history but is a separate illustrated publication.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Inspected PDF pages 2–5 (PDF lines 28–141): values, migration and subsistence narrative, treaty summary, Sandy Lake account, 1863–64 non-removal history, allotment and boarding-school discussion. Other pages were not reviewed. Treaty details were not independently checked against full primary records in this pass.

Review recorded: October 22, 2026
